title: Unit I — Hardness and EDTA
intro: Hardness, units, three worked problems and EDTA estimation. Includes the complete supplied Unit I question bank; remaining revision topics are pending.

sections.title: Hardness: temporary and permanent
paragraphs: Hardness is the property of water that prevents ready lathering with soap. Dissolved calcium and magnesium salts react with soap to produce insoluble scum. Soft water readily gives lather; hard water does not.
Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of higher fatty acids such as stearic, palmitic or oleic acid. Calcium and magnesium ions precipitate the corresponding insoluble soaps.

Temporary hardness, also called carbonate or alkaline hardness, is mainly due to calcium and magnesium bicarbonates. Boiling decomposes these bicarbonates and precipitates calcium carbonate or magnesium hydroxide.

Permanent hardness, also called non-carbonate or non-alkaline hardness, is caused by chlorides, sulphates and nitrates of calcium and magnesium. Boiling does not remove it; softening processes are required.

sections.title: Calcium-carbonate equivalents and units
paragraphs: Express the hardness-producing salts on one common basis: their equivalent concentration as calcium carbonate. For the divalent calcium and magnesium salts used in these problems, multiply each salt concentration by 100 and divide by its molecular mass.

Add the bicarbonate contributions for temporary hardness. Add the chloride, sulphate and nitrate contributions for permanent hardness. Total hardness is the sum of temporary and permanent hardness. Sodium/potassium salts and suspended matter do not contribute to the calcium/magnesium hardness calculation.

For dilute water samples, 1 mg/L is approximately 1 ppm. One degree French represents 10 ppm as calcium carbonate; one degree Clarke represents approximately 14.3 ppm. The supplied notes use the rounded conversion 1 ppm = 0.07 °Clarke.

examples.title: Problem 1
question_paragraphs: A water sample contains Ca(HCO₃)₂ = 4.86 g/L, Mg(HCO₃)₂ = 5.84 g/L, CaSO₄ = 6.80 g/L and MgSO₄ = 8.40 g/L. Calculate temporary and permanent hardness in degrees French and Clarke.
paragraphs: PankusDesk-completed working, using the supplied problem and CaCO₃-equivalent table.
\(\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}:4860\times\dfrac{100}{162}=3000\) mg/L as CaCO₃.
\(\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}:5840\times\dfrac{100}{146}=4000\) mg/L as CaCO₃.
\(\mathrm{CaSO_4}:6800\times\dfrac{100}{136}=5000\) mg/L as CaCO₃.
\(\mathrm{MgSO_4}:8400\times\dfrac{100}{120}=7000\) mg/L as CaCO₃.
Temporary hardness = 3000 + 4000 = 7000 ppm. French = 7000/10 = 700 °Fr; Clarke ≈ 7000 × 0.07 = 490 °Cl.
Permanent hardness = 5000 + 7000 = 12000 ppm. French = 12000/10 = 1200 °Fr; Clarke ≈ 12000 × 0.07 = 840 °Cl.

examples.title: Problem 2
question_paragraphs: Calculate temporary and permanent hardness for Ca(HCO₃)₂ = 162 mg/L, Mg(HCO₃)₂ = 73 mg/L, CaSO₄ = 136 mg/L, MgCl₂ = 95 mg/L, CaCl₂ = 111 mg/L, NaCl = 100 mg/L and suspended matter = 50 mg/L.
paragraphs: PankusDesk-completed working, using the supplied problem and CaCO₃-equivalent table.
\(\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}:162\times\dfrac{100}{162}=100\) mg/L as CaCO₃.
\(\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}:73\times\dfrac{100}{146}=50\) mg/L as CaCO₃.
\(\mathrm{CaSO_4}:136\times\dfrac{100}{136}=100\) mg/L as CaCO₃.
\(\mathrm{MgCl_2}:95\times\dfrac{100}{95}=100\) mg/L as CaCO₃.
\(\mathrm{CaCl_2}:111\times\dfrac{100}{111}=100\) mg/L as CaCO₃.
NaCl and suspended matter are excluded from the hardness sum.
Temporary hardness = 100 + 50 = 150 ppm. Permanent hardness = 100 + 100 + 100 = 300 ppm. Total = 150 + 300 = 450 ppm.
examples.final_answer: Temporary hardness = 150 ppm; permanent hardness = 300 ppm; total hardness = 450 ppm.

examples.title: Problem 3
question_paragraphs: Determine total hardness in degrees French and Clarke for MgCl₂ = 19 ppm, MgSO₄ = 12 ppm, Ca(NO₃)₂ = 16.4 ppm, NaOH = 40 ppm, KOH = 56 ppm, suspended matter = 100 ppm, Ca(HCO₃)₂ = 162 ppm and Mg(NO₃)₂ = 14.8 ppm.
paragraphs: PankusDesk-completed working, using the supplied problem and CaCO₃-equivalent table.
\(\mathrm{MgCl_2}:19\times\dfrac{100}{95}=20\) ppm as CaCO₃.
\(\mathrm{MgSO_4}:12\times\dfrac{100}{120}=10\) ppm as CaCO₃.
\(\mathrm{Ca(NO_3)_2}:16.4\times\dfrac{100}{164}=10\) ppm as CaCO₃.
\(\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}:162\times\dfrac{100}{162}=100\) ppm as CaCO₃.
\(\mathrm{Mg(NO_3)_2}:14.8\times\dfrac{100}{148}=10\) ppm as CaCO₃.
NaOH, KOH and suspended matter are excluded from the hardness sum.

discrepancy.label: Source discrepancy
discrepancy.message: The question prints Mg(HCO₃)₂ = 14.6 mg/L, but the table uses 146 mg/L and gives 100 mg/L as its CaCO₃ equivalent. At 14.6 mg/L the equivalent would be 10 mg/L. The question also includes CaCO₃ and HCl, while the printed table does not account for HCl. The intended treatment needs confirmation; neither printed value has been silently changed.

sections.title: Estimation of hardness by the EDTA method
paragraphs: EDTA estimation is a complexometric titration. Calcium and magnesium ions form complexes with disodium ethylenediaminetetraacetate. An ammonia–ammonium chloride buffer maintains the required pH, approximately 10.
Take a known volume of the water sample, add the buffer and Eriochrome Black-T (EBT) indicator. The metal–indicator complex is wine red. Titrate with standard EDTA solution.
The metal–EDTA complex is more stable than the metal–indicator complex. EDTA binds the metal ions, releasing the blue indicator. The endpoint is the change from wine red to blue.

For permanent hardness, boil the sample for about 30 minutes to remove temporary hardness, then titrate with EDTA. Temporary hardness is the difference between total and permanent hardness. The method is rapid, convenient and accurate.
notes: Volumes in this expression are in mL. The supplied expression uses EDTA normality, not molarity; those quantities must not be interchanged without the corresponding equivalence convention.
